I've been farming these 12 mu in Quzhou for over forty years, and after studying agriculture at the vocational college in Handan back in the 1980s, I learned to calculate my inputs by target yield rather than just copying my neighbors. My wheat went in last October on 8 mu — I rotary tilled before sowing and used an improved semi-dwarf variety like Shimai 22 or Liangxing 99 at about 30 jin per mu. I'm targeting 500 kg/mu, so I'll apply 18 kg N per mu total: roughly 10 kg N from a compound fertilizer basal application that also gives me 6 kg P₂O₅ and 4 kg K₂O, then topdress with urea at jointing for the remaining 8 kg N. I'll irrigate four times including the winter irrigation already done, with the remaining three at green-up, jointing, and grain filling — water is expensive from the tube well, but a yield loss costs me more than the pumping. For the summer maize on that same 8 mu, the turnaround after wheat harvest is barely six days, so no-tillage direct seeding is the only practical choice. I'll plant a hybrid like NK815 or Nongda 372, apply 16 kg N split between basal and the big flare stage, plus 5 kg P₂O₅ and 4 kg K₂O, and irrigate twice during the critical periods. I'm keeping 4 mu in cotton as my price-risk hedge — seed cotton has held around 3 yuan per jin, and while it needs more labor and about 10 pesticide sprays for bollworm and aphids, it diversifies my income. I'll rotary till the cotton ground in April, plant a hybrid variety, apply 14 kg N, 5 kg P₂O₅, and 5 kg K₂O per mu, and irrigate twice. My yield expectations are 500 kg/mu for wheat, 550 kg/mu for maize, and 320 kg/mu for seed cotton — I've learned to be conservative, especially with groundwater restrictions tightening every year and my pumping costs rising.
